Introduction

AgentGuard brings observability, security, governance, and quality into one trust layer for AI agents.

sections.title: What is AgentGuard?
sections.text:
## What is AgentGuard?

AgentGuard is an AI trust platform for teams building agents and LLM applications. It unifies observability, runtime guardrails, security testing, and governance in one console — so you can ship faster without trading off control or auditability.

Observability: Traces, spans, sessions, cost, and latency across every model and tool call.

Security: Guardrails, OWASP LLM coverage, red teaming, and incident visibility.

Governance: Compliance frameworks, audit trail, AI BOM, and policy-as-code.

Quality: Scores, LLM Evals evals, Test Sets, and human review queues.

Design principle: Policy and guardrails are configured in the console and enforced at runtime through the SDK — you tune behavior without redeploying agent code for every rule change.

sections.title: Platform areas
sections.text:
## Platform areas

The console is organized into areas that map to how teams operate day to day.

Area: Control Plane | What you do there: Dashboards, widgets, trust profile rollup | Typical users: Platform owners, leadership

Area: Observability | What you do there: Trace Explorer, sessions, users, spend signals | Typical users: Engineers, SRE, support

Area: Evaluation | What you do there: Scores, eval jobs, datasets, human review | Typical users: ML engineers, quality teams

Area: Security | What you do there: Guardrails, OWASP, red teaming, incidents | Typical users: Security engineers, AppSec

Area: Governance | What you do there: Compliance, audit trail, AI BOM, data governance | Typical users: GRC, auditors, compliance

### How data flows

- Your application calls an LLM or tool through the AgentGuard SDK (or public ingestion API).

- Traces and guardrail outcomes are sent to AgentGuard storage (PostgreSQL + ClickHouse).

- The console surfaces traces, security findings, and governance evidence in real time.

- RBAC controls who can view or change each area; entitlements and instance controls can further limit modules on your plan or deployment.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.text:
## Introduction

AgentGuard is a trust layer for AI agents. A single init() at startup auto-instruments your existing LLM clients, so every call is both traced into the AgentGuard console and guarded by server-configured guardrails that can redact or block prompts and responses.

Observability: Traces, spans, tokens, latency and cost for every LLM & tool call.

Guardrails & Security: PII, secrets, prompt-injection, toxicity, budget and tool-permission checks.

Cost: Per-call, per-user and per-feature spend, normalized across providers.

Governance: Policy configured server-side and applied live — tune without redeploying.

What onboarding means here: four steps — install the SDK → configure your project keys → instrument your LLM client → see traces in the console. There are no per-call code changes.

Good to know: AgentGuard is provider-agnostic (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, Gemini, and framework agents), and prompt/response content is NOT captured by default — you record only model, tokens, latency, cost and guardrail findings until you explicitly opt in.

Throughout this guide, code samples show both stacks. Use the language toggle to switch. Package names: @actaclad/agentguard (Node) and actaclad-agentguard → import agentguard (Python).

sections.title: Quick Start
sections.text:
## Quick Start

The fast path — copy-paste and you should see your first trace in a few minutes. Each step shows Node.js and Python.

1. Install the SDK

Node.js example
```bash
npm install @actaclad/agentguard
# or: pnpm add @actaclad/agentguard
```

2. Get your keys from the console

In the AgentGuard console, open Project Settings → API Keys, click Create API Key, and copy your Public Key and Secret Key — plus your Host URL and Project ID. You’ll paste these into your env file in the next step.

3. Set your project keys (env)

Copy these from your AgentGuard project in the console. The same four variables work for both SDKs.

Environment variables
```bash
AGENTGUARD_PUBLIC_KEY=pk-lf-...
AGENTGUARD_SECRET_KEY=sk-lf-...
AGENTGUARD_BASE_URL=https://<your-agentguard-host>
AGENTGUARD_PROJECT_ID=<project-id>    # enables live guardrail polling
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...                 # your provider key, unchanged
```

4. Initialize & instrument your LLM client

Call init() once at startup, before you make LLM calls.

Node.js example
```typescript
import OpenAI from "openai";
import * as agentguard from "@actaclad/agentguard";

agentguard.init();                    // once, at startup — keys/base/project from env
agentguard.instrumentOpenAI(OpenAI);  // explicit class = ESM/bundler-safe (recommended)

const openai = new OpenAI();
```

5. Run your app — attach context with withPolicy

Wrap your call in withPolicy (Node) / policy() (Python) to attach who and what the call is for: userId (the end user), feature, and a metadata bag for tenant and any custom business dimensions. Then use your LLM client exactly as before — the call is traced and guarded. For short-lived scripts, call flush() before exit so batched spans are sent.

Node.js example
```typescript
const res = await agentguard.withPolicy(
  { userId: "user-123", feature: "checkout-assistant", metadata: { tenant: "acme" } },
  () => openai.chat.completions.create({
    model: "gpt-4o",
    messages: [{ role: "user", content: "summarise the crew roster" }],
  }),
);

await agentguard.flush();   // flush telemetry before the process exits
```

One channel for context: Anything extra you want attached to a call — user, tenant, feature, custom tags — goes inside withPolicy (via metadata). It’s the one place to add context. The tenant key is metadata.tenant, and feature is written by the SDK as metadata.feature_name plus a feature: trace tag.

6. View traces in the console

Open your AgentGuard host, pick your project, and go to Traces. Your run appears with model, tokens, latency, cost and any guardrail findings.

sections.text:
## Detailed onboarding

The same path, expanded — with the what, the why, and the options at each step.

### Prerequisites

You need an AgentGuard project and its credentials. The SDK does not create organizations or projects — create or select the project in the console first, then copy its keys.

- Public key (pk-lf-…) and secret key (sk-lf-…) — from the project’s API-keys page.

- Host URL — your AgentGuard base URL (cloud or self-hosted / BYOC).

- Project ID — enables live guardrail-config polling. Without it, tracing still works but guardrails are disabled and a warning is logged.

- Your existing provider key (e.g. OPENAI_API_KEY) — unchanged.

### Install

Install the core SDK, plus only the provider/framework extras you actually use — peer deps are optional.

Node.js example
```bash
npm install @actaclad/agentguard          # core (npm)
pnpm add @actaclad/agentguard             # core (pnpm)

# optional peer deps — install only what you use:
npm install openai
npm install @anthropic-ai/sdk
npm install @aws-sdk/client-bedrock-runtime
npm install @modelcontextprotocol/sdk     # MCP tools
npm install @langchain/core               # LangChain / LangGraph tools
```

Node.js ships provider support as optional peer deps — install openai, @anthropic-ai/sdk, @aws-sdk/client-bedrock-runtime, @modelcontextprotocol/sdk or @langchain/core only as needed. Guardrails need no extra install.

### Configure

Most values can come from an environment variable or be passed to init() directly — an explicit init() argument always wins over the env var. Aliases AGENT_GUARD_* are also accepted.

Variable: AGENTGUARD_PUBLIC_KEY | Purpose: Project public API key (pk-lf-…). | SDK: Both

Variable: AGENTGUARD_SECRET_KEY | Purpose: Project secret API key (sk-lf-…). | SDK: Both

Variable: AGENTGUARD_BASE_URL | Purpose: AgentGuard host URL. Set this one. Node still reads the legacy AGENTGUARD_HOST, but only when AGENTGUARD_BASE_URL is unset. | SDK: Both

Variable: AGENTGUARD_PROJECT_ID | Purpose: Enables live guardrail-config polling. Without it, tracing works but guardrails are off. | SDK: Both

Variable: AGENTGUARD_CAPTURE_CONTENT | Purpose: true to record prompt/response text on traces. Off by default. | SDK: Both

Variable: AGENTGUARD_KILL_SWITCH_POLLER_ENABLED | Purpose: false turns off the 10-second kill-switch check. The switch is then read only with the regular config poll. | SDK: Both

Variable: AGENTGUARD_INCLUDE_INFRA_SPANS | Purpose: true to keep infra spans (DB/HTTP/RPC), which are dropped by default. | SDK: Both

### Options on init()

The options most teams set. Node uses camelCase (onBlock), Python uses snake_case (on_block).

Option: projectId | Default: env | Meaning: Turns on guardrails. Without it you get tracing only.

Option: environment | Default: production | Meaning: A label on every trace, for filtering. It does not change which guardrails run.

Option: guardrails | Default: auto | Meaning: auto enforces. observe runs every guardrail and records what it finds, but blocks nothing (redaction still applies). off instruments nothing: no guardrails and no automatic tracing.

Option: onBlock | Default: raise | Meaning: What a block does, on input and output: raise throws AgentGuardBlocked; refuse returns a refusal message as the response.

Option: tracing | Default: batch | Meaning: batch for production; realtime sends each span at once, for debugging.

Option: pollInterval | Default: 900 | Meaning: Seconds between guardrail-config refreshes.

Option: killSwitchPollInterval | Default: 10 | Meaning: Seconds between kill-switch checks.

Scoping: Guardrails are set per project in the console. Use one project per environment (dev, staging, prod). If a guardrail seems inactive, check that the SDK points at the project where you turned it on.

### Instrument LLM providers

After init(), provider calls are traced and guarded automatically. Instrument the providers you use:

OpenAI — chat + voice

Node.js example
```typescript
import OpenAI from "openai";
agentguard.init();
agentguard.instrumentOpenAI(OpenAI);  // covers chat completions AND audio (STT/TTS)
```

Why pass the class?: In ESM/bundled apps, require("openai") and your import OpenAI can resolve to different module copies, so passing the exact class you imported — instrumentOpenAI(OpenAI) — removes that ambiguity. Same for instrumentAnthropic(Anthropic). instrumentOpenAI covers chat completions and audio (STT/TTS).

### Anthropic (incl. Bedrock / Vertex)

Node.js example
```typescript
import Anthropic from "@anthropic-ai/sdk";
agentguard.init();
agentguard.instrumentAnthropic(Anthropic);  // also covers AnthropicBedrock / AnthropicVertex
```

### AWS Bedrock (Node only)

Two ways, depending on how you get your client — add middleware to a client you own, or patch the class so every client (e.g. LangChain’s internal one) is covered. In a bundled app, reach for instrumentBedrockClient first.

Node.js example
```typescript
import * as Bedrock from "@aws-sdk/client-bedrock-runtime";
import { instrumentBedrock, instrumentBedrockClient } from "@actaclad/agentguard/bedrock";

agentguard.init();

// (a) You own the client instance — add middleware to it:
const client = new Bedrock.BedrockRuntimeClient({ region: "us-east-1" });
instrumentBedrockClient(client);

// (b) You DON'T hold the client (e.g. LangChain's ChatBedrockConverse builds
//     its own) — patch the class so EVERY client is covered:
instrumentBedrock(Bedrock);
```

Bundlers: Under Next.js, webpack or Turbopack, the file that constructs the client can resolve to a different module instance of @aws-sdk/client-bedrock-runtime than the file that calls instrumentBedrock — so patching the class in one file does not reach a client built in the other, and the calls go out untraced with nothing in the log to say so. Call instrumentBedrockClient(client) where the client is constructed. Keep instrumentBedrock as well only if a framework builds a client you never hold (ChatBedrockConverse); the two must not both cover the same client.

Bedrock model ids are normalized so cost matches server-side (Claude ids resolve to canonical names). An InvokeModelCommand carrying an embeddings body is recorded as llm.bedrock.embedding: guardrails are skipped (there is no conversation to read) and usage comes from the provider’s embedding token count.

Provider names: Azure, Bedrock and Vertex clients report their real provider: azure, bedrock or vertex (not openai / anthropic). List those models under the matching provider in Allowed Model List.

### Trace your agent / framework

For multi-step agents, tie everything into a single trace with identity attached.

### LangGraph.js (Node)

createLangGraphHandler() returns a real LangChain callback handler that reconstructs the full graph → node → llm/tool trace. Pair it with startTrace so tracing and enforcement land in one trace:

LangGraph handler
```typescript
import { createLangGraphHandler } from "@actaclad/agentguard/langgraph";
import { withPolicy } from "@actaclad/agentguard";

agentguard.init();

// One linked trace: pair startTrace + the handler so tracing (handler) and
// enforcement (instrumented model clients) land in a SINGLE trace.
const session = agentguard.startTrace({
  name: "sick-call-triage",
  userId: controllerId,
  sessionId,
  feature: "sick-call-triage",
  metadata: { tenant: "PTY-Hub", provider },
});

const handler = createLangGraphHandler({
  root: session.root,
  userId: controllerId,
  sessionId,
  feature: "sick-call-triage",
});

const final = await withPolicy(
  { userId: controllerId, sessionId, feature: "sick-call-triage", onBlock: "refuse" },
  () => session.run(() => graph.invoke(initial, { callbacks: [handler] })),
);

session.update({ output: { outcome, summary } });
await agentguard.flush();
console.log(session.url ?? session.id);
```

Note: Enforcement inside graph nodes comes from the model layer, not the handler (LangChain callbacks are observe-only). ChatOpenAI is covered via the shared openai package; ChatBedrockConverse via instrumentBedrock(...). Tools need their own wrapper; see the next section.

### Guard your tools (Node)

Model calls are guarded once you instrument the provider. Tool calls are not guarded until you wrap them. Pick the line that matches how your agent runs tools:

Node.js example
```typescript
import { guardTools, runTool } from "@actaclad/agentguard/tools";
import { instrumentMcpClient } from "@actaclad/agentguard/mcp";

agentguard.init();

// LangChain / LangGraph tools
const tools = guardTools([search, refundOrder]);

// MCP servers: after connect()
instrumentMcpClient(mcpClient);

// Your own tool loop (e.g. Bedrock Converse)
const result = await runTool(use.name, use.input, (args) => myTools[use.name](args));
```

On every tool call, Excessive Agency decides whether the agent may use the tool, and blocked tools never run. The arguments and the result are scanned. The call appears as a tool.<name> span under the graph step that ran it.

### Manual traces & spans

To group work under one named trace with your own identity/metadata:

Node.js example
```typescript
const session = agentguard.startTrace({ name: "chat-request", userId });
// ... run instrumented LLM/tool calls inside ...
await session.run(() => handleRequest());
session.update({ output: { answer } });
await agentguard.flush();
```

### Guardrails & policy

Which guardrails run is decided server-side, per project, in the console — the SDK polls that config and applies it, so you enable, disable or tune a guardrail with no client redeploy. Code can only narrow the server set (disable a named guardrail for a scope), never add one that isn’t enabled.

There are 13 built-in guardrails, plus a kill switch and your own custom policies. See Guardrails — availability & configuration (#guardrail-config) for the full list.

### Per-request policy & identity

Attach identity/attribution and override policy for a block of code. onBlock:"refuse" returns a refusal message instead of throwing, on both input and output:

Node.js example
```typescript
import { withPolicy } from "@actaclad/agentguard";

await withPolicy(
  { userId: req.user.id, sessionId: req.session.id,
    feature: "triage", onBlock: "refuse",   // synthetic refusal instead of throw
    disable: ["toxic-content"] },           // narrow the guardrail set here
  async () => handleRequest(),
);
// onBlock: "raise" (default) throws AgentGuardBlocked.
```

### Try a policy before you enforce it

With guardrails: "observe", every guardrail runs and records its findings, but nothing is blocked. Blocks show as WOULD BLOCK in the console. Read a few days of findings, then switch to auto.

Node.js example
```typescript
agentguard.init({ guardrails: "observe" });
```

### Kill switch

Turn on the kill switch in the console to block every model call in the project with your message. This stops your agents. Running apps pick it up within about 10 seconds, with no redeploy. If AgentGuard can’t be reached, the last known state stays in force.

### Capturing content

By default AgentGuard records model, tokens, latency, cost and guardrail findings — but not the prompt/response text (a PII-safe default). To store input/output content on traces:

Environment variables
```bash
# Off by default. Enable to store prompt/response text on traces:
AGENTGUARD_CAPTURE_CONTENT=true
```

Privacy: Content is captured after input guardrails run, so PII redaction is reflected in what’s stored. For streamed responses, only the input is captured (the response streams after the span closes). Keep this flag off in regulated environments unless you have a reason to store text.

Scanning is separate: PII, prompt injection and toxic content are checked by your AgentGuard host, so the SDK sends that text there even with capture off. The text is scanned and not stored.

### Verify in the console

Confirm the loop end-to-end: open your host, select the project, and check these views.

### Production checklist

- Flush on shutdown. Call flush() (Node) / agentguard.flush() (Python) before the process exits or between short-lived runs so batched spans are sent.

- Point at the right host. For self-host / BYOC, set AGENTGUARD_BASE_URL to your deployment, not the default cloud host.

- Set project_id. Required for guardrails — without it you get tracing only.

- Pick your tracing mode. batch in production; realtime only for debugging.

- Decide on content capture. Leave AGENTGUARD_CAPTURE_CONTENT off unless you need text and have handled privacy.

- Handle secrets properly. Keep keys in env/secret manager; never commit them. Keep your environment variable templates documented for the team.

- One project per environment. Point dev, staging and prod at separate projects so their guardrails and traces stay apart.

- Roll out guardrails in observe mode first, then switch to auto.

- Guard your tools. Wrap tools with guardTools, runTool or the MCP instrumentation (Node). Python guards LangChain and CrewAI tools automatically; MCP needs instrument_mcp_client.

### Explicit / provider-agnostic calls via agentguard.chat()

When you want AgentGuard to make the call (provider-agnostic via LiteLLM) or to reach a provider without an auto-instrumentor:

Python example
```python
resp = agentguard.chat(
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}],
    model="gpt-4o",
    user_id="u-123", session_id="s-456", feature="chat",
    metadata={"tenant": "acme"},

# achat(...) is the async equivalent — same guardrails + tracing.
```

Python example
```python

    agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "..."}]})

agentguard.flush()
# To pass the handler yourself: config={"callbacks": [agentguard.langchain_handler()]}
# To turn automatic tracing off: policy(autotrace=False)
```

Python example
```python
# MCP tools  ->  pip install "actaclad-agentguard[mcp]"
from agentguard.mcp import instrument_mcp_client
instrument_mcp_client(session)   # permission check, argument and result scans

agentguard.instrument_crewai()          # [crewai]
agentguard.instrument_openai_agents()   # [openai-agents]
```


### Guardrails & policy

Which guardrails run is decided server-side, per project, in the console — the SDK polls that config and applies it, so you enable, disable or tune a guardrail with no client redeploy. Code can only narrow the server set (disable a named guardrail for a scope), never add one that isn’t enabled.

There are 13 built-in guardrails, plus a kill switch and your own custom policies. See Guardrails — availability & configuration (#guardrail-config) for the full list.

### Per-request policy & identity

Attach identity/attribution and override policy for a block of code. onBlock:"refuse" returns a refusal message instead of throwing, on both input and output:

Python example
```python
with agentguard.policy(
    user_id="u-123", session_id="s-456", feature="chat",
    metadata={"tenant": "acme"},
    disable=["toxic-content"],   # narrow the guardrail set for this scope only
    on_block="refuse",           # or "raise" (default) -> AgentGuardBlocked
):
    resp = OpenAI().chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4o", messages=[...])
```

### Try a policy before you enforce it

With guardrails: "observe", every guardrail runs and records its findings, but nothing is blocked. Blocks show as WOULD BLOCK in the console. Read a few days of findings, then switch to auto.

Python example
```python
agentguard.init(project_id="...", guardrails="observe")   # SDK 1.7.0+
```

### Kill switch

Turn on the kill switch in the console to block every model call in the project with your message. This stops your agents. Running apps pick it up within about 10 seconds, with no redeploy. If AgentGuard can’t be reached, the last known state stays in force.

### Capturing content

By default AgentGuard records model, tokens, latency, cost and guardrail findings — but not the prompt/response text (a PII-safe default). To store input/output content on traces:

Environment variables
```bash
# Off by default. Enable to store prompt/response text on traces:
AGENTGUARD_CAPTURE_CONTENT=true
```

Privacy: Content is captured after input guardrails run, so PII redaction is reflected in what’s stored. For streamed responses, only the input is captured (the response streams after the span closes). Keep this flag off in regulated environments unless you have a reason to store text.

Scanning is separate: PII, prompt injection and toxic content are checked by your AgentGuard host, so the SDK sends that text there even with capture off. The text is scanned and not stored.

### Verify in the console

Confirm the loop end-to-end: open your host, select the project, and check these views.

### Production checklist

- Flush on shutdown. Call flush() (Node) / agentguard.flush() (Python) before the process exits or between short-lived runs so batched spans are sent.

- Point at the right host. For self-host / BYOC, set AGENTGUARD_BASE_URL to your deployment, not the default cloud host.

- Set project_id. Required for guardrails — without it you get tracing only.

- Pick your tracing mode. batch in production; realtime only for debugging.

- Decide on content capture. Leave AGENTGUARD_CAPTURE_CONTENT off unless you need text and have handled privacy.

- Handle secrets properly. Keep keys in env/secret manager; never commit them. Keep your environment variable templates documented for the team.

- One project per environment. Point dev, staging and prod at separate projects so their guardrails and traces stay apart.

- Roll out guardrails in observe mode first, then switch to auto.

- Guard your tools. Wrap tools with guardTools, runTool or the MCP instrumentation (Node). Python guards LangChain and CrewAI tools automatically; MCP needs instrument_mcp_client.

sections.title: Guardrails — availability & configuration
sections.text:
## Guardrails — availability & configuration

What each guardrail checks, where it runs, and what it needs to fire.

Both SDKs run the same guardrails. You turn them on and tune them in the console, under Guardrails. To see a project’s live config: GET {host}/api/public/guardrails?projectId=<id> (basic auth pk:sk).

### The 13 guardrails

Guardrail: PII Redaction | SDK name: pii-redaction | Checks: input + output | Runs: AgentGuard service | Typical action: Redact · Block · Audit | Needs: —

Guardrail: Prompt Injection Detection | SDK name: prompt-injection | Checks: input | Runs: AgentGuard service | Typical action: Block · Flag | Needs: —

Guardrail: Toxic / Harmful Content | SDK name: toxic-content | Checks: input + output | Runs: AgentGuard service | Typical action: Block · Flag | Needs: —

Guardrail: Secrets Scanner | SDK name: secret-scanner | Checks: input + output | Runs: in your app | Typical action: Block · Flag | Needs: Passwords are opt-in: select Passwords under secret types

Guardrail: Token Scanner | SDK name: token-scanner | Checks: input + output | Runs: in your app | Typical action: Block · Flag | Needs: —

Guardrail: Token Limit | SDK name: token-limit | Checks: input | Runs: in your app | Typical action: Block | Needs: a limit

Guardrail: Allowed Model List | SDK name: allowed-model-list | Checks: input | Runs: in your app | Typical action: Block · Flag | Needs: a model list

Guardrail: Output Schema Validation | SDK name: schema-validation | Checks: output | Runs: in your app | Typical action: Block · Repair | Needs: a schema

Guardrail: Rate Limit Guard | SDK name: rate-limit | Checks: input | Runs: AgentGuard service | Typical action: Block | Needs: limits

Guardrail: Budget Guard | SDK name: budget-guard | Checks: input | Runs: AgentGuard service | Typical action: Block | Needs: a budget

Guardrail: Execution Limit Guard | SDK name: execution-limit-guard | Checks: input + output | Runs: in your app | Typical action: Block · Flag | Needs: limits (depth, calls, tools per turn, duration, repeated calls)

Guardrail: Hallucination Detection | SDK name: hallucination | Checks: output | Runs: in your app | Typical action: Block · Flag | Needs: a judge model: your own model client is used

Guardrail: Excessive Agency | SDK name: tool-permission | Checks: tool calls | Runs: in your app | Typical action: Allow · Read-only · Needs approval · Block | Needs: tool rules; max tool calls per turn (default 10)

Where it runs: In your app means the SDK checks the text itself, with no network call. AgentGuard service means the SDK sends the text to your AgentGuard host and gets a score back. PII, prompt injection and toxic content are checked in one call per step. There is nothing extra to install in your app.

### Also enforced

- Kill switch. Blocks every model call in a project with your message, which stops your agents. The SDK checks it every 10 seconds, so it takes effect without a redeploy. If the check fails, the last known state stays in force.

- Custom policies. Your own keyword or regex rules, created in the console. Each one blocks or flags a match.

### Tool calls

When a tool is guarded, the SDK checks it in three steps. First, Excessive Agency checks whether the agent may use the tool. Then the arguments are scanned before the tool runs, and the result is scanned before the model sees it. PII, secrets, tokens, prompt injection and toxic content apply here.

For JSON arguments and results, prompt injection and toxic content read only the sentences (three words or more). Dates, IDs and codes are not scored, so plain tool data is not flagged. Findings appear under the tool span and name the tool and side.

### Old names

Older projects may still use a name from the left column. The SDK ignores those names, logs an “enabled but no detector registered” warning, and never runs the check. Rename them to the current name.

Old name: secrets-token-scanner | Current name(s): secret-scanner + token-scanner

Old name: allowlist | Current name(s): allowed-model-list

Old name: schema | Current name(s): schema-validation

Old name: hallucination-guard | Current name(s): hallucination

### “Enabled but not firing” — checklist

- Old name. The guardrail uses a name from the table above. Rename it.

- Wrong direction. The guardrail is off for the side you are testing. For example, prompt injection checks input only, and hallucination checks output only.

- The AgentGuard service could not be reached. PII, prompt injection and toxic content then let the call through, and the SDK logs a warning. Check that your AgentGuard host is reachable and that its guardrail service is running.

- The action is Flag, not Block. A flag records a flagged finding and lets the call continue. Set the action to block if you want the call stopped.

- Observe mode is on. Nothing is blocked. Findings that would have blocked show as WOULD BLOCK.

- Nothing was found. The text was clean, so there is no finding.

### How guardrails are scoped

- Per project and per direction. A guardrail runs whenever it is on, for the input side, the output side, or both.

- One project per environment. Use separate projects for dev, staging and prod to keep policies, traces and cost apart.

- The environment you pass to init() is a label. It tags traces for filtering. It does not decide whether a guardrail runs.

sections.title: Troubleshooting / FAQ
sections.text:
## Troubleshooting / FAQ

Q: No traces are showing up in the console.
A:

Check, in order: (1) init() runs before your first LLM call; (2) AGENTGUARD_PUBLIC_KEY, AGENTGUARD_SECRET_KEY and AGENTGUARD_BASE_URL are set and point at the correct host; (3) you called flush() before a short-lived process exits (batched spans are lost otherwise); (4) you’re looking at the right project.

Q: A guardrail I enabled isn't firing.
A:

Check that AGENTGUARD_PROJECT_ID is set and points at the project where you turned the guardrail on. Config refreshes every 15 minutes (pollInterval), so wait or restart the app. Code can only turn guardrails off for a scope; it can’t add one. For more, see the “Enabled but not firing” checklist.

Q: PII, injection or toxicity checks pass without scanning.
A:

These three are checked by your AgentGuard host. If the SDK can’t reach it, the call goes through unchecked and the SDK logs a warning. Check that AGENTGUARD_BASE_URL is right and that the host’s guardrail service is running. There is nothing to install in your app.

Q: Plain tool data (dates, IDs) was flagged as injection.
A:

Update the Node SDK to 3.2.2 or later. It reads only the sentences in JSON tool arguments and results, so dates, IDs and codes are no longer scored.

Q: Prompt and response text isn't visible on my traces.
A:

That’s the default — content capture is off for privacy. Set AGENTGUARD_CAPTURE_CONTENT=true to store input/output text. Content is recorded after input guardrails, so redactions are reflected; for streamed responses only the input is captured.

Q: A guardrail blocked a call and my code threw an exception.
A:

The default onBlock is raise, so a block throws AgentGuardBlocked, on input or output. Catch it, or set refuse (in init(), withPolicy() or policy()) to get a refusal message instead. To see what would be blocked without blocking, use observe mode. An input block happens before the model call, so it costs no tokens.

Q: Do I have to change every call site to add tracing?
A:

No. A single init() (plus instrument*(Class) on Node) auto-instruments your existing clients — no per-call changes. Use withPolicy() / policy() or startTrace() only when you want to attach identity or group a multi-step run into one trace.

Q: Are the two SDKs identical?
A:

The core is the same: init(), traces, the same guardrails set in the console, observe mode, the kill switch, and content capture off by default. Differences: Node adds the Bedrock runtime client, LangGraph.js and OpenAI voice, uses explicit instrument*(Class) calls, and wraps tools with guardTools / runTool. Python auto-detects providers (including Gemini), guards LangChain and CrewAI tools automatically, and offers agentguard.chat() plus CrewAI and OpenAI Agents tracing.

Q: How do guardrail changes reach a running app?
A:

Without a redeploy. The SDK refreshes guardrail config every 15 minutes and checks the kill switch every 10 seconds. If a check fails, the last known config stays in force.

Control Plane

The cross-pillar view: where you look first, what changed, and whether the platform as a whole is healthy.

sections.title: What the Control Plane is for
sections.text:
## What the Control Plane is for

One place to stand before you know which pillar the question belongs to.

The other four sections each answer a specific kind of question. The Control Plane exists for the moment before that — when you want to know whether anything needs attention at all. It summarises across observability, quality, security and governance, and hands you off to whichever one owns the detail.

Page: Overview | What it answers: Is the platform healthy, and which pillar should I open first? | Who opens it: Anyone, daily

Page: Dashboards | What it answers: How do our own metrics look, arranged our way? | Who opens it: Platform owners

Page: Trust Profile | What it answers: How trustworthy is this project, and on which axis is it weak? | Who opens it: Leadership, GRC

sections.title: Overview
sections.text:
## Overview

The daily starting point — recent activity, spend, and anything flagged across the platform.

A digest rather than a report: traffic and cost trends, recent traces, and whatever is currently drawing attention from the other pillars. Every tile links to the page that owns it, so treat this as a routing screen rather than somewhere to investigate.

sections.title: Dashboards
sections.text:
## Dashboards

Your own charts over your own trace data, saved and shared.

Build widgets from the metrics AgentGuard already collects — volume, latency, cost, token usage, scores — and arrange them into dashboards per team or per application. Widgets are defined once and reusable across dashboards.

### How to use it

1. Start from a widget, not a dashboard

Widgets carry the query. Build the one chart you actually want to watch first, then place it — it will be available to every dashboard.

2. Scope with the environment filter

Mixing staging and production in one chart is the most common reason a dashboard looks wrong. Filter by environment early.

sections.title: Trust Profile
sections.text:
## Trust Profile

A composite Trust Rating across the dimensions that make an AI system trustworthy — and an honest blank where we cannot measure one.

Eight of the nine dimensions are computed from live signals: trace error rates, latency distribution, evaluation scores, guardrail configuration and violations, compliance coverage, data-policy adherence, audit-chain integrity and ownership completeness on your AI inventory. Only Adversarial Resistance is still underived, and it says so rather than being folded into the score.

Blank is not zero: A dimension with no data stays blank and says why. Scoring it zero would assert you did badly at something that was never measured, which is exactly the kind of number this platform is meant not to produce.

### The nine dimensions

Every dimension is scored 0–100 over the same 30-day window, or left blank. The third column is the one to read when a dimension says insufficient data — it is the condition that has not been met yet, and the page repeats the specific shortfall next to the badge.

Dimension: Reliability
Observability | What it measures: The share of traced operations that finished without an error. | Moves off “insufficient data” when: Any traced observation in the window. | Anchored in: NIST AI RMF 1.0 §3.1 (https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/3-sec-characteristics/) · Google SRE, Monitoring Distributed Systems (https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/)

Dimension: Performance
Observability | What it measures: Whether latency is predictable relative to itself — not whether it is fast. | Moves off “insufficient data” when: 20 completed generations in the window. | Anchored in: Google SRE, Monitoring Distributed Systems (https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/) · Dean & Barroso, The Tail at Scale (CACM, 2013) (https://cacm.acm.org/research/the-tail-at-scale/)

Dimension: Correctness
Evaluation | What it measures: The average quality your evaluators report. | Moves off “insufficient data” when: One evaluator score in the window. Only scores with source EVAL count — scores pushed through the API or added by hand do not. | Anchored in: NIST AI RMF 1.0 §3.1 (https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/3-sec-characteristics/) · ISO/IEC 25059:2023 (https://www.iso.org/standard/80655.html) · EU AI Act Art. 15 (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj)

Dimension: Stability
Evaluation | What it measures: Whether evaluation quality is holding up over time, or quietly regressing. | Moves off “insufficient data” when: A single evaluator with at least 5 scores in each half of the window — in practice, one that has been running for more than half the window (about 15 days of 30). | Anchored in: NIST AI RMF 1.0 §3.1 (https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/3-sec-characteristics/) · EU AI Act Art. 72 (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj)

Dimension: Safety
Security | What it measures: How much of the guardrail catalogue is switched on, and how clean your traffic is against it. | Moves off “insufficient data” when: Configuring any guardrail, or any traffic arriving — whichever happens first. | Anchored in: NIST AI RMF 1.0 §3.2 (https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/3-sec-characteristics/) · NIST AI 600-1 (2024) (https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1) · OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025) (https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/)

Dimension: Adversarial Resistance
Security | What it measures: How the system holds up under deliberate attack. | Moves off “insufficient data” when: The red-team integration shipping. No project setting will change it before then. | Anchored in: NIST AI RMF 1.0 §3.3 (https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/3-sec-characteristics/) · OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026) (https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/) · MITRE ATLAS (https://atlas.mitre.org/) · EU AI Act Art. 15 (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj)

Dimension: Compliance
Governance | What it measures: How much of the mapped control set your runtime can actually evidence. | Moves off “insufficient data” when: Any runtime evidence — a guardrail decision, an eval result or an inventory observation. Project and API-key setup records alone do not score. | Anchored in: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 (https://www.iso.org/standard/42001) · NIST AI RMF 1.0 (https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/3-sec-characteristics/) · EU AI Act Arts. 9–15 (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj) · CSA AI Controls Matrix v1.1 (2026) (https://cloudsecurityalliance.org/artifacts/ai-controls-matrix-v1-1)

Dimension: Data Governance
Governance | What it measures: Whether your traffic adhered to the data policy you actually stated. | Moves off “insufficient data” when: A residency policy AND evidence matching one of its measures. Today the workable path is “require redaction before egress” plus PII actually being detected in your traffic. | Anchored in: EU AI Act Art. 10 (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj) · NIST AI RMF 1.0 §3.6 (https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/3-sec-characteristics/) · NIST AI 600-1 (2024) (https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1)

Dimension: Accountability
Governance | What it measures: Whether the AI systems you run have named owners, and whether the audit record is intact. | Moves off “insufficient data” when: At least one system appearing in the AI Bill of Materials. | Anchored in: NIST AI RMF 1.0 §3.4 (https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/3-sec-characteristics/) · EU AI Act Art. 12 (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj)

### How each score is calculated

No dimension is a subjective rating. Each is an arithmetic result over evidence already in your project, stated here in full so a number can be argued with.

Reliability

1 − (ERROR-level observations ÷ all observations), as a percentage.

- Filter Observability → Traces to level ERROR to see exactly what is failing.

- This counts what your application reported to the SDK. A provider timeout you caught and retried successfully never reaches the trace as an error, so this measures user-visible failure, not provider flakiness.

Performance

p95 ÷ p50 over completed generations, mapped so a ratio of 2× or less scores 100 and 10× or worse scores 0.

The p95 ÷ p50 ratio itself is an AgentGuard construct. The sources support percentile-based latency, not this specific ratio.

- A healthy LLM workload sits around 1.5–3× on its own, purely from output-length variance. Past roughly 5×, the cause is usually queueing, retries or timeouts rather than the model.

- There is deliberately no SLO to configure. One absolute latency threshold cannot be right for both a nightly batch summariser and a realtime voice agent, and requiring every project to define one is why this dimension used to read blank indefinitely.

- Only completed generations count. Spans wrap arbitrary application code, and an unfinished observation is excluded rather than counted as instant.

Correctness

Count-weighted mean of every eval score in the window, normalised to 0–1 (a value above 1 is read as a 0–100 scale and divided accordingly).

- Attach evaluators in AI Quality. Each evaluator's scores pool into this number weighted by how many it produced, so a high-volume evaluator moves it more than a rarely-run one.

- A low number here is a genuine quality signal rather than a configuration gap — open the evaluator with the worst mean rather than adding more evaluators.

Stability

The window is split in half at its midpoint. For every evaluator with at least 5 scores in BOTH halves, regression = max(0, earlier mean − later mean). The score is (1 − the mean of those regressions) × 100.

Deliberately not called robustness: NIST §3.1 defines robustness as maintaining performance under a variety of circumstances, whereas this dimension measures whether quality regresses over time.

- Getting better is never penalised. Scores that rise rate the same 100 as scores that hold perfectly steady, because only regression is measured.

- Each evaluator is compared only against itself. Adopting a new, stricter evaluator mid-window therefore cannot register as a quality regression, which matters because adding evaluators is exactly what we ask you to do.

- An evaluator that ran in only one half is skipped rather than treated as a shift. Continuous running is what unlocks this dimension, not volume.

Safety

Mean of two halves, over whichever has data: guardrail coverage (enabled ÷ 12 in the catalogue) and clean-traffic rate (1 − violations ÷ observations).

- Enable more of the 12 catalogue guardrails. Coverage needs no traffic at all, so this half moves the moment you configure something.

- This is deliberately not a pass rate. A guardrail that runs and passes records nothing, so passed ÷ total cannot be computed — under that formula a perfectly clean project would score zero.

- A project that has never configured a guardrail scores on traffic alone: never-configured is an absence of evidence, not evidence of zero protection.

Adversarial Resistance

Not yet derived. Unlike the other eight, there is no signal anywhere in the platform to compute this from.

- There is nothing to configure. This one is on us, and it is listed as insufficient data rather than hidden so that the Trust Rating is visibly incomplete instead of quietly rounded up.

Compliance

(covered + ½ × partial) ÷ in-scope controls, across every framework in the crosswalk. Controls AgentGuard structurally cannot evidence are excluded from the denominator rather than counted as failures.

- Open the framework you are assessed against and work its gaps. Every derivable control states the evidence that would satisfy it.

- Coverage reports what is evidenced, not what is configured. A guardrail that is enabled but never exercised is green on the OWASP page and a gap here — the two are legitimately allowed to disagree.

Data Governance

Mean of up to three adherence measures, over whichever have evidence: residency (in-region ÷ region-known flows), PII redaction (findings redacted or blocked ÷ all PII findings), and denied-provider (traffic that avoided providers the policy forbids).

- Set the policy in Governance → Data Governance. Enabling the PII guardrail under Security does not feed this dimension: adherence is measured against a stated policy, and without one there is nothing to adhere to.

- PII findings exist only where PII was detected. A genuinely PII-free window leaves this blank rather than scoring it, which is the same reason a clean guardrail window is not treated as proof.

- Residency and denied-provider adherence both need region and provider attribution on your traffic, which arrives with the gateway.

Accountability

Mean of owner completeness (systems with an owner ÷ all systems) and audit-chain integrity (verified = 100, broken = 0). Integrity joins the average only once there are audit events to verify.

- Assign owners in Governance → AI Bill of Materials. That half of the score is entirely within your control and usually the fastest point on this page to move.

- An empty inventory stays blank rather than scoring. A verified hash chain over zero events is not evidence that everything is owned — it is the absence of anything to be accountable for.

### How nine become one

The Trust Rating is the weighted mean of whichever dimensions are measured. A blank dimension is not scored as zero — its weight is redistributed across the rest, so the headline always describes what was actually observed. The weight shown beside each dimension is the one in force for your project’s preset.

Confidence reports how much of the picture is filled in: high when at least 8 of the 9 dimensions are measured, medium at 5, low below that. A high score at low confidence is a thin result, not a good one — which is the reason the badge sits next to the number rather than in a tooltip.

Critical findings override the average: An open critical incident, a mandatory control gap or a high-severity exploitable red-team finding caps the number at 60 and the band at Limited assurance, regardless of the weighted mean, and each one carries an additional penalty. A single unresolved critical issue is not something a good average should be able to average away — in NIST’s words, trustworthiness is only as strong as its weakest characteristics.

### Trust Rating bands

The headline is a band, with the number beneath it. Bands are deliberately coarse: a weighted mean over nine dimensions cannot support the difference between 73 and 74, and a band does not pretend it can. The same bands appear on the Overview, the Trust Profile and every Trust Report.

Band: High assurance | Trust Rating: 90–100 | Notes:

Band: Strong assurance | Trust Rating: 75–89 | Notes:

Band: Moderate assurance | Trust Rating: 60–74 | Notes: Not reachable while a critical issue is open.

Band: Limited assurance | Trust Rating: 40–59 | Notes: The ceiling while any critical issue is open.

Band: High risk | Trust Rating: 0–39 | Notes:

Band: Not assessed | Trust Rating: — | Notes: No dimension had evidence. Unmeasured, not unsafe.

When Confidence is low — fewer than 5 of the 9 dimensions measured — the band is marked provisional. It is still the honest reading of what was observed, but it describes less than half of the picture.

### Standards and methodology

No published standard defines an AI trust rating. What the standards do define is what AI trustworthiness consists of, and how a composite indicator should be built. Each dimension is anchored in the first — see the Anchored in column above — and the way nine become one follows the second:

Method choice: Weighted mean, missing dimensions excluded | Anchored in: OECD/JRC Handbook on Constructing Composite Indicators (2008) (https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2008/08/handbook-on-constructing-composite-indicators-methodology-and-user-guide_g1gh9301/9789264043466-en.pdf) | What the source says: Normalisation, weighting, aggregation, missing-data treatment and sensitivity analysis

Method choice: Critical issues cap the rating | Anchored in: NIST AI RMF 1.0 §3 (https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/airmf/3-sec-characteristics/) | What the source says: Trustworthiness “is only as strong as its weakest characteristics”

Method choice: Critical issues cap the rating | Anchored in: Qualys SSL Labs, SSL Server Rating Guide (https://github.com/ssllabs/research/wiki/SSL-Server-Rating-Guide) | What the source says: Specific flaws cap the grade regardless of the numeric score

Method choice: Weight presets by risk profile | Anchored in: OpenSSF Scorecard (https://github.com/ossf/scorecard/blob/main/README.md) | What the source says: Individually scored checks combined as a risk-weighted average

Method choice: Number reported with a band | Anchored in: FIRST CVSS v4.0 Specification (https://www.first.org/cvss/v4.0/specification-document) | What the source says: Numeric score reported alongside a qualitative severity band

Method choice: Number reported with a band | Anchored in: MLCommons AILuminate v1.0 (2025) (https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.05731) | What the source says: AI safety results published as qualitative grades

Method choice: “Assurance” band vocabulary | Anchored in: UK DSIT, Introduction to AI Assurance (2024) (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/introduction-to-ai-assurance/introduction-to-ai-assurance) | What the source says: Assurance as measuring, evaluating and communicating trustworthiness

Two dimensions depart from the standards’ own vocabulary, and say so in their formulas above: Stability measures regression over time, which NIST treats under reliability rather than robustness, and Performance uses a latency tail ratio of our own construction. Weights and presets are versioned, and the version in force is printed on every Trust Profile and Trust Report.

What the Trust Rating does not cover yet: NIST AI RMF 1.0 lists seven characteristics of trustworthy AI. Two have no dimension yet: fair, with harmful bias managed (§3.7), and explainable and interpretable (§3.5). They are named here so that a rating is never read as covering them.

### How to use it

1. Read the blanks before the scores

Most blanks close faster than a score already being measured moves — attach an evaluator, enable a guardrail, assign owners in the AI Bill of Materials. Two are exceptions worth recognising: Stability needs an evaluator running across more than half the window before any comparison exists, and Adversarial Resistance cannot be unlocked from your side at all.

2. Follow the weakest measured dimension

Each one names the signal behind it, so you can go straight to the page that produces that signal rather than guessing.

sections.title: Common questions
sections.text:
## Common questions

Q: Everything reads zero or “—”. Is something broken?
A: Almost certainly not. Every number here is derived from traces, so nothing appears until your application sends some. Start with Onboarding; once a single traced call lands, these views populate on the next load.

Q: How is the Overview different from the Observability overview?
A: This one spans all four pillars — a little of each. The Observability overview goes deep on traffic, latency, cost and errors alone. Open this to decide where to look; open that one when you already know it is a traffic or performance question.

Q: Why is a Trust Profile dimension blank rather than zero?
A: Blank means insufficient data, and it is deliberately distinct from a score of zero. Zero would claim you did badly at something we never measured. Each blank dimension states what is missing — usually an evaluator, a guardrail, or ownership on your AI systems.

Q: Is the Trust Rating based on a published standard?
A: No published standard defines an AI trust rating. Each dimension is anchored in published standards — NIST AI RMF 1.0, ISO/IEC 42001 and 25059, the EU AI Act, OWASP — and the way nine dimensions become one follows established practice for composite indicators. Both are listed, with links, under Standards and methodology.

sections.title: Observability
sections.text:
Observability

What your agents actually did — every call, its inputs and outputs, what it cost, and how long it took.

sections.title: What Observability is for
sections.text:
## What Observability is for

Answering “what happened?” without adding print statements to production.

An agent run is a tree of decisions — model calls, tool calls, retries, branches — and when the result is wrong, the interesting part is usually several levels down. Observability records that tree as it happens, with the content, the token usage and the timing attached, so a failure can be read rather than reproduced.

Everything else builds on this: Evaluation scores attach to observations. Guardrail decisions and compliance evidence are derived from the same trace stream. If tracing is not flowing, most of the platform has nothing to work from.

Page: Overview | What it answers: Is traffic, latency, cost or error rate off? | Who opens it: Engineers, SRE

Page: Trace Explorer | What it answers: What exactly happened on this request? | Who opens it: Engineers, support

Page: Sessions | What it answers: How did this whole conversation go? | Who opens it: Support, product

Page: Users | What it answers: What is one user's experience and cost? | Who opens it: Support, finance

Page: Prompts | What it answers: Which prompt version is in production, and how is it doing? | Who opens it: Engineers, prompt authors

Page: Playground | What it answers: What would a change to this prompt do? | Who opens it: Prompt authors

sections.title: Overview
sections.text:
## Overview

Traffic, latency, cost and errors over time, with the models and prompts behind them.

The shape of your traffic and what it is costing you, broken down by model and environment. Use it to notice that something changed; use the Trace Explorer to find out what.

sections.title: Trace Explorer
sections.text:
## Trace Explorer

Every request as a tree of observations, with inputs, outputs, timing and cost at each node.

A trace is one end-to-end run; the observations inside it are the individual model and tool calls. Open a trace to see the sequence, how long each step took, and what was actually sent and returned — with any guardrail decisions and evaluation scores attached to the step they belong to.

### How to use it

1. Filter before you scroll

Filter by environment, user, session, model or score. Reading traces in time order rarely finds anything on a busy project.

2. Work down the tree, not across the list

When a run produced a wrong answer, the cause is usually one level deeper — a tool returning something unexpected, or a retry that changed the prompt. Expand rather than moving to the next trace.

3. Follow the trace into the other pillars

Scores show what an evaluator made of the output; guardrail findings show what was caught. Both link back here, so investigations converge on the same view.

sections.title: Sessions
sections.text:
## Sessions

Multiple traces grouped into one conversation, in order.

A chat has many requests but one thread. Passing a session id groups them, so you can read a conversation the way the user experienced it rather than as scattered traces — which is usually the only way to see where a multi-turn interaction went wrong.

sections.title: Users
sections.text:
## Users

Activity, cost and quality for one end user.

When you attach a user id, this becomes the per-user view: what they did, what it cost, and how their outputs scored. It is the fastest route from a support ticket to the traces behind it.

sections.title: Prompts
sections.text:
## Prompts

Prompts as versioned artefacts, fetched at runtime rather than pasted into code.

Manage prompts here and fetch them from the SDK, and each version is linked to the generations it produced. That link is what makes “this got worse after the prompt change” answerable rather than a suspicion. Labels let you promote a version to production without a deploy.

### How to use it

1. Fetch by label, not by version number

Point your application at a label such as production. Promoting a new version then becomes a change here rather than a code release.

2. Compare versions on scores, not impressions

Each version carries the generations it produced and their scores. Compare those before promoting.

sections.title: Playground
sections.text:
## Playground

Try a prompt against a model before committing it.

Edit a prompt, run it against a configured model, and see the result with its token usage and cost — without shipping anything. Useful for the quick “does this wording help?” loop; for a real answer across many cases, use a dataset run in AI Quality instead.

sections.title: Common questions
sections.text:
## Common questions

Q: My application ran but no trace appeared. Where did it go?
A: Three usual causes, in order of likelihood: the SDK has no credentials (it warns at startup under [agentguard] if so), the process exited before the batched exporter flushed, or the environment filter on this page excludes it. Call flush() before exit in short-lived scripts.

Q: Cost shows zero for a model I know is billable.
A: Cost is computed from token usage against a model price table. A model the table does not recognise records usage but no cost. Either the model name is arriving in an unexpected form, or it needs adding to the price list — the generation’s model field tells you which.

Q: Why are my turns not grouped into one session?
A: Sessions group by the session id you supply. If it is absent or a new one is generated per turn, each turn becomes its own session. Pass a stable id for the length of the conversation.

Q: Prompts show no usage even though the app is running.
A: Usage is linked when a generation is produced from a prompt fetched through the SDK. Prompts pasted into your code as strings cannot be linked — fetch them with getPrompt() and the connection is made automatically.

sections.title: AI Quality
sections.text:
AI Quality

Whether the output was any good — scored automatically, by people, or against a fixed set of cases.

sections.title: What AI Quality is for
sections.text:
## What AI Quality is for

Turning “it seems worse since Tuesday” into a number you can act on.

Observability tells you what an agent did; it cannot tell you whether the answer was correct, grounded, or useful. That judgement has to come from somewhere — a model acting as judge, a person reviewing, or a fixed set of cases with known-good answers. This section is those three sources and the scores they produce.

Page: Decision Models | What it answers: Score every trace, not a sample, without the LLM bill | Who opens it: ML engineers, platform owners

Page: Human Evals | What it answers: Get people to judge the cases that matter | Who opens it: Quality teams, domain experts
