sections.title: Overview
sections.text:
## Overview

Score trends across evaluators, and what is dragging them.

Where quality is heading over time, per evaluator. A step change here usually lines up with a prompt or model change — cross-reference the Prompts page for the version that landed at the same moment.

sections.title: Scores
sections.text:
## Scores

Every score, with the trace and observation it was given to.

The raw record: evaluator name, value, and the exact observation it judged. Filter to one evaluator and sort by value to find the worst cases — that list is usually more informative than the average.

Scores attach to observations: A score belongs to a specific step of a run, not to the run as a whole. That is what lets you tell a bad retrieval from a bad final answer in the same trace.

sections.title: LLM Evals
sections.text:
## LLM Evals

A model scoring your outputs continuously, against criteria you write.

Define what good looks like as a prompt template, point it at the traffic you care about with a filter, and every matching observation gets scored as it arrives. This is the main source of scores on a live system.

### How to use it

1. Narrow the filter before you widen it

Start with one route or one prompt. An evaluator pointed at everything produces a number that averages away the thing you were looking for — and costs the most to run.

2. Sample rather than score everything

Every evaluation is a billed model call. A sample is usually enough to see a trend, and costs a fraction of full coverage. To score everything instead, put a decision model (#decision-models) in front of the judge.

3. Read the reasoning on disagreements

When a score looks wrong, the judge’s own reasoning usually shows that the rubric was ambiguous rather than the output bad. Fix the template before trusting the trend.

sections.title: Decision Models
sections.text:
## Decision Models

A fast, low-cost model answers first. Your LLM judge only sees the cases it is unsure about.

An LLM judge reads each output and writes a verdict. That is thorough, but every call costs money, which is why most teams only score a sample. A decision model is built for one job: answering a clear question such as “does this answer contain false claims?” It replies with how likely the answer is yes, in a fraction of a second, for a small fraction of the cost of an LLM call.

Think of a triage nurse and a doctor. The nurse settles the clear cases on the spot and sends only the unclear ones to the doctor. AgentGuard works the same way: the decision model handles the cases it is sure about, and the rest go to your LLM judge. You keep the judge’s quality where it matters and can score all of your traffic instead of a sample.

### How it works

Step: 1. A trace arrives | What happens: Your evaluator picks it up as usual.

Step: 2. The decision model answers | What happens: It returns a probability from 0 to 1, for example 0.97 = “almost certainly yes”.

Step: 3. Sure enough? Done | What happens: If it is confident enough (your threshold), that probability is saved as the score.

Step: 4. Unsure? Ask the judge | What happens: Otherwise the same evaluation goes to your LLM judge, exactly as before.

Step: Something fails? | What happens: The LLM judge takes over. An evaluation is never dropped because of the decision model.

Example, a Hallucination evaluator asking “The generation contains false claims”:

Answer being checked: “The capital of Australia is Sydney.” | Decision model: 0.97, very sure it's false | Outcome: Score 0.97. Judge not needed.

Answer being checked: “The capital of Australia is Canberra.” | Decision model: 0.02, very sure it's fine | Outcome: Score 0.02. Judge not needed.

Answer being checked: “Mona Lisa was painted in the early 1600s.” | Decision model: 0.55, unsure | Outcome: Sent to the LLM judge, which scores it.

Several evaluators, one call: When several evaluators run on the same trace, their questions go to the decision model together in a single request, so adding another evaluator adds very little cost.

### Set it up

1. Connect a decision model

Go to Settings → LLM Connections → Decision Models, click Add decision model, choose TypeSafe Jev and paste its API key. The key is checked when you save.

2. Keep a strong LLM judge

The LLM judge is the backup for every case the decision model is unsure about, so the project still needs a normal LLM connection (OpenAI, Anthropic and so on). Make its model a strong one, such as a gpt-4.1 class model: it only sees the hard cases, and on those a small model is little better than a guess.

3. Library evaluators are already set up

Evaluators in the Evaluator Library marked with a blue ⚡ (hover it to see “Decision-ready”) start using the decision model as soon as it is connected, with a confidence threshold of 0.2. There is nothing to clone or edit. For your own evaluators, open the template and set the Confidence threshold and a decision question (#decision-question). To use a different threshold on a library evaluator, clone it and change it there.

4. Run it on traces, at 100%

Create the evaluator on Traces with sampling at 100%. Coverage is the point: the decision model makes scoring every trace affordable.

Confidence threshold: Empty | What it means: Off. The evaluator uses only the LLM judge.

Confidence threshold: 0 | What it means: Never escalate. The decision model answers everything.

Confidence threshold: 0.2 (library default) | What it means: Only the genuinely unsure cases go to the judge, typically a small share.

Confidence threshold: 0.6 | What it means: More cases go to the judge: higher cost, more written reasoning.

What “confidence” means: Confidence is how far the answer is from a coin flip. A probability of 0.5 has confidence 0; 0.9 or 0.1 has confidence 0.8; 1.0 or 0.0 has confidence 1. With a threshold of 0.2, anything between 0.4 and 0.6 goes to the judge.

### Writing the question

The Decision question field on the template is what the decision model is asked. Your LLM judge still gets the full prompt. Leave it empty and the decision model reads the prompt instead, but a short statement works better. Three rules:

1. One statement, true or false

Write a single sentence that is either true or false for an answer. No instructions, examples or “think step by step”.

2. True means a score of 1

The decision model returns how likely the statement is true, and that becomes the score. If a score of 1 means “toxic”, the statement must say toxic, not polite.

3. Use the prompt's variable names

Refer to the data by the names the prompt uses, such as generation, query or context. A {{variable}} the prompt does not have is refused, because the decision model would never receive it.

Evaluator (1 means…): Toxicity (1 = toxic) | Good question: “The generation contains offensive or demeaning content.” | Avoid: “Is the generation polite?” gives the opposite score

Evaluator (1 means…): Groundedness (1 = grounded) | Good question: “Every claim in the generation is supported by the context.” | Avoid: “Check each claim against the context and explain.”

Evaluator (1 means…): Refusal (1 = refused) | Good question: “The generation declines to answer the query.” | Avoid: “Rate how helpful the answer is from 1 to 10.”

### Reading the results

You see: score: 0.97 · confidence 0.94 · jev-1.13.0 | It means: Decided by the decision model.

You see: A written sentence of reasoning | It means: The decision model was unsure (or unavailable), so the LLM judge scored it.

You see: An error on the decision model's row in Settings | It means: Its last call failed. Evaluations are running on the LLM judge until it recovers.

Scores can mean slightly different things: A decision model answers “how likely is it true”; an LLM judge often answers “how much”. For yes/no evaluators the two agree. For “how helpful” style scores, keep in mind that one evaluator’s scores may come from both.

sections.title: Human Review
sections.text:
## Human Review

Queues of items for people to judge, with the results stored as scores like any other.

Some judgements need a domain expert — a clinician, a lawyer, a support lead. Queue the items, let reviewers work through them, and their verdicts land as scores alongside the automated ones. Also the honest way to check whether your judge agrees with people.

sections.title: Test Sets
sections.text:
## Test Sets

A fixed set of inputs, with expected outputs where you have them.

Production traffic changes from day to day, so scoring it can never isolate the effect of your change. A dataset holds the inputs still. Run a version against it, run the next version against the same cases, and the difference is attributable.

### How to use it

1. Build it from real failures

The most valuable Test Set items are traces that went wrong in production. Add them from the Trace Explorer as you find them, and the set grows into a regression suite for the failures you actually have.

2. Attach evaluators to the run

A run without scoring only tells you it completed. Attach the same evaluators you use in production so the comparison is like for like.

sections.title: Experiments
sections.text:
## Experiments

Compare runs against a Test Set, side by side.

Two prompt versions, two models, or two agent configurations over the same Test Set, with their scores next to each other. This is where a promotion decision gets made on evidence rather than on the impression left by a handful of examples.

sections.title: Common questions
sections.text:
## Common questions

Q: I created an evaluator but no scores are appearing.
A: An evaluator only runs on observations its filter matches, and only on traffic that arrives after it was created unless you run it over historic data explicitly. Check the filter first — an over-narrow one is the usual cause — then confirm traces are arriving at all.

Q: The same trace has two scores from one evaluator.
A: Scoring is idempotent per observation: a span that is ingested twice is evaluated once. The deliberate exception is the Run Evaluation batch action, which re-scores on request and appends a new score alongside the old one — so two scores from an explicit re-run are expected.

Q: Does LLM Evals cost money?
A: Yes — each evaluation is a model call billed to the API key you configure. Sampling exists for this reason: scoring a representative share of traffic usually answers the question at a fraction of the cost of scoring all of it. A decision model (#decision-models) changes that trade-off: it answers most evaluations for a small fraction of the cost, so scoring all traffic becomes affordable.

Q: What happens if the decision model is down or my key expires?
A: Nothing is lost. Every evaluation it cannot answer goes to the evaluator’s LLM judge instead, exactly as if no decision model were set. The error appears on the decision model’s row in Settings → LLM Connections and clears on its own once it answers again.

Q: Which evaluators should use a decision model?
A: Ones that ask a clear yes/no or pick-one question: is it toxic, is it grounded in the context, did the agent refuse, which category is this. Keep the LLM judge alone for open-ended rubrics that need written reasoning, for “rate this 1 to 10” style scores, and for categories where several can apply at once.

Q: When should I use a Test Set instead of scoring production?
A: Use production scoring to find out whether quality is drifting. Use a dataset when you want to compare two versions on identical inputs — the only way to attribute a change to your edit rather than to different traffic.

sections.title: Security
sections.text:
Security

Stopping the things an agent should not do — and proving you tried, with red-team runs and an incident record.

sections.title: What Security is for
sections.text:
## What Security is for

An agent that can be talked into anything is a liability, however good its answers are.

The failure modes here are adversarial rather than accidental: someone talking your agent past its instructions, personal data leaving in a prompt, a credential echoed back in a response, an agent reaching for a tool it was never meant to touch. This section is the controls that catch those inline, plus the exercises that test whether they hold.

Enforcement is in the SDK: Guardrails run in your application, around each model and tool call, which is what lets a request be blocked rather than only recorded. PII, prompt injection and toxic content are scored by your AgentGuard host; the SDK makes the decision. You configure guardrails in the console, and the enforcement comes with the SDK version you deploy.

Page: Overview | What it answers: What has been caught, and how often? | Who opens it: Security engineers

Page: Guardrails | What it answers: What is switched on, and what is it finding? | Who opens it: Security, platform owners

Page: OWASP LLM Top 10 | What it answers: Which industry-standard risks have a control configured? | Who opens it: Security, AppSec

Page: Red Teaming | What it answers: Do the controls hold under deliberate attack? | Who opens it: Security engineers

Page: Security Incidents | What it answers: What needs following up, and did we? | Who opens it: Security, GRC

sections.title: Overview
sections.text:
## Overview

Findings over time, by category and by outcome.

What guardrails have caught recently, grouped by category and by what happened — blocked, redacted, or recorded. A spike in one category is usually more informative than the total.

sections.title: Guardrails
sections.text:
## Guardrails

Thirteen inline controls, each switched on per project with its own action.

Every guardrail follows the same shape: enable it, choose what happens when it triggers, and read its findings. Each has a detail page with its own configuration, recent findings and traces — so the walkthrough below applies to all of them, and the table is the index.

### The thirteen guardrails

Guardrail: PII Redaction | What it catches: Personal data in requests and responses | Applies to: Input, output

Guardrail: Prompt Injection | What it catches: Attempts to override your instructions | Applies to: Input

Guardrail: Toxic / Harmful Content | What it catches: Abusive or unsafe content | Applies to: Input, output

Guardrail: Secrets Scanner | What it catches: Credentials and API keys | Applies to: Input, output

Guardrail: Token Scanner | What it catches: Access tokens and bearer credentials | Applies to: Input, output

Guardrail: Token Limit | What it catches: Requests exceeding a token ceiling | Applies to: Input

Guardrail: Rate Limit | What it catches: Too many requests in a window | Applies to: Input

Guardrail: Budget Guard | What it catches: Spend beyond a configured cap | Applies to: Input

Guardrail: Allowed Model List | What it catches: Calls to models outside your approved list | Applies to: Input

Guardrail: Output Schema Validation | What it catches: Responses that break the expected shape | Applies to: Output

Guardrail: Hallucination Detection | What it catches: Claims unsupported by the provided context | Applies to: Output

Guardrail: Execution Limit Guard | What it catches: Runaway agents: too many steps, calls or repeated tool calls | Applies to: Input, output

Guardrail: Excessive Agency | What it catches: Tool calls an agent is not permitted to make | Applies to: Tool calls

### How to use it

1. Start in observe mode

Observe records findings and changes nothing your users see: set guardrails: "observe" in the SDK, and blocks show as WOULD BLOCK. Run it for a few days first — the false-positive rate on your own traffic is the only one that matters, and it is cheap to learn before you start blocking.

2. Read findings before choosing an action

Each detail page lists what was caught, with the trace behind it. Move to redact or block once the findings look right, not before.

3. Handle blocks in your application

A blocking guardrail raises to the caller. Decide what the user should see — a refusal, a retry, a fallback — rather than letting the exception surface raw. To stop an agent at once, use the kill switch: it blocks every model call in the project within about 10 seconds.

sections.title: OWASP LLM Top 10
sections.text:
## OWASP LLM Top 10

The industry-standard risk list, mapped to the controls you have switched on.

LLM01 through LLM10 with the AgentGuard control that addresses each, so you can answer “what are you doing about prompt injection?” without assembling it by hand. Useful for security reviews and vendor questionnaires.

Configured, not evidenced: This page reflects configuration — whether a control is switched on. Governance › Compliance reflects evidence — whether it was observed running. The two can legitimately disagree, and neither is wrong when they do.

sections.title: Red Teaming
sections.text:
## Red Teaming

Attack your own agent on purpose, and see what gets through.

Configured guardrails are a claim; a red-team run is the test. Adversarial prompts are fired at your agent across vulnerability categories, and the run reports what was caught and what was not. Each result links to its trace, so a bypass can be read rather than guessed at.

### How to use it

1. Run against staging first

A red-team run generates deliberately hostile traffic and real model spend. Point it at a non-production environment unless you have a reason not to.

2. Treat a bypass as a finding, not a score

The value is in the specific prompt that got through. Open its trace, confirm the gap, and adjust the guardrail or the system prompt.

3. Re-run after changes

A run is a point-in-time result. Re-running after a prompt or model change is what turns it into a regression check.

sections.title: Security Incidents
sections.text:
## Security Incidents

The findings that need a human decision, tracked to closure.

Most guardrail findings are routine and need no follow-up. The ones that do belong here, with their severity and status, so an auditor can see not only what was detected but what was done about it.

sections.title: Common questions
sections.text:
## Common questions

Q: Where do guardrails actually run?
A: In the SDK, inside your application process, before and after the model call. That is what allows a request to be blocked rather than merely recorded — but it also means a guardrail fix reaches you through an SDK upgrade, not a platform deploy.

Q: A guardrail is enabled but never fires.
A: Check three things in order: that the SDK version you run includes it, that traffic goes through the SDK rather than straight to the provider, and that the guardrail’s scope matches the direction you expect — some apply to inputs, some to outputs, some to both.

Q: Why does OWASP show green while Compliance shows a gap?
A: They answer different questions. This page reports what is configured — whether a guardrail is switched on. Compliance reports what is evidenced — whether it was observed running. A guardrail enabled but never exercised is legitimately green here and a gap there.

Q: Will turning a guardrail on break my application?
A: It depends on the action you choose. Observe-only records findings and changes nothing. Redact rewrites content in place. Block raises to the caller, which your application must be ready to handle — start in observe mode, read a few days of findings, then decide.

sections.title: Governance
sections.text:
Governance

Turn what your agents actually did into evidence an auditor will accept — compliance coverage, AI inventory, data flows, and a tamper-evident record.

sections.title: What Governance is for
sections.text:
## What Governance is for

Proving to someone else — an auditor, a regulator, a customer's security team — that your AI systems are controlled.

The other pillars help you build and operate. Governance answers a different question: can you show it? It turns activity that already happened — guardrail decisions, evaluation results, the models you actually called, every configuration change — into evidence, maps that evidence to the control frameworks auditors ask about, and keeps a tamper-evident record of it.

Evidence, not intent: Governance never asks you to declare what you do. It reports what your runtime actually did. A control you have configured but never exercised is not counted as covered.

Page: Overview | What it answers: Where do we stand right now? | Who opens it: Anyone

Page: Compliance | What it answers: How much of each framework can we evidence? | Who opens it: GRC, auditors

Page: Policy as Code | What it answers: What rules will govern tenants? (Preview) | Who opens it: Platform owners

Page: AI Bill of Materials | What it answers: What AI systems do we actually run, and who owns them? | Who opens it: GRC, platform owners

Page: Data Governance | What it answers: Where does our data flow, and what is the residency policy? | Who opens it: Privacy, GRC

Page: Audit Trail | What it answers: What happened, and can we prove the record is intact? | Who opens it: Auditors, security

sections.title: Overview
sections.text:
## Overview

The one screen to open first — current posture across every Governance area.

Compliance status and framework coverage, policy distribution, recent risks and audit events, and your AI assets by type — each card links through to the page that owns it. Use it as a starting point, not a report: the detail lives one click deeper.

### How to use it

1. Check whether coverage is being measured at all

If frameworks read Not Assessed rather than a percentage, no runtime evidence has arrived in the selected window. Send traffic through the SDK first — nothing else on this page will be meaningful until then.

2. Follow the weakest framework

Click through to Compliance and open the framework with the lowest coverage. Framework pages list the specific controls that are short of evidence.

sections.title: Compliance
sections.text:
## Compliance

Coverage against EU AI Act, ISO/IEC 42001, NIST AI RMF, OWASP LLM Top 10, India DPDP and FAA 14 CFR Part 5 — derived from evidence, not from a questionnaire.

Every control is mapped to the runtime events that would prove it. A control is satisfied when matching evidence actually arrives in the selected window. Three levels: the index shows all frameworks, a framework page shows its controls, and a control page shows the evidence behind one control and how it has moved over time.

### The four control statuses

Status: Covered | Meaning: Matching evidence arrived in this window. | Counts toward coverage: Yes — in full

Status: Partial | Meaning: The right kind of evidence is flowing, but not the specific signal this control needs. | Counts toward coverage: Yes — as a half

Status: Gap | Meaning: No matching evidence. Usually something to turn on. | Counts toward coverage: Yes — as a zero

Status: Out of scope | Meaning: Cannot be proven from runtime at all, e.g. training-data provenance. | Counts toward coverage: No — excluded entirely

Why out-of-scope is excluded: Coverage is (covered + ½ × partial) ÷ in-scope controls. Controls AgentGuard structurally cannot evidence are left out of the denominator rather than counted as failures — you are never penalised for something no amount of configuration could close.

### “Not Assessed” vs 0%

With no runtime activity in the window, frameworks read Not Assessed and no overall score is shown. A brand-new project has configuration records from the moment it is created, and scoring those would manufacture a number that describes nothing. A percentage appears once real guardrail, evaluation or model-inventory activity exists.

Compliance vs OWASP LLM Top 10: The Security section’s OWASP page reports what is configured — whether a guardrail is switched on. Compliance reports what is evidenced — whether it was observed running. The two can legitimately disagree: a guardrail enabled but never exercised is green on one page and a gap on the other.

### How to use it

1. Start from the framework, not the control list

Open the framework you are being assessed against. Its page ranks controls by status, so the gaps are at your fingertips.

2. Open a gap and read the recommendation

Every derivable control states what evidence would satisfy it and what to do — usually enabling a guardrail or attaching an evaluator. The control page also breaks down which expected event kinds arrived and which did not.

3. Check the trend before you act

The control page shows status across recent windows. A control that was covered last month and is a gap now is a regression, not a missing feature — treat it differently.

4. Export an evidence pack

Export evidence pack on the Compliance index produces the current coverage with its supporting evidence, for an auditor or an internal review.

Coverage indicators, not certification: These views describe what your runtime can demonstrate. They are not a certification, an audit opinion, or legal assurance of compliance with any framework.

sections.title: Policy as Code
sections.text:
## Policy as Code

Per-tenant rules in YAML, version-controlled in Git and reviewed in pull requests.

Preview — sample data: This page previews the planned experience. The policies shown are sample data: they are not evaluated against your traffic and nothing on this page is enforced. It is here so you can see the shape of the feature and tell us whether the model fits how you work.

The intent is that policies live beside your code — declared in YAML, scoped with a condition such as tenant tier or environment, reviewed through the same pull-request process as everything else, and then evaluated in the gateway on every request.

Until this ships, enforcement lives in the Security section: Guardrails is where rules actually run against traffic today.

sections.title: AI Bill of Materials
sections.text:
## AI Bill of Materials

A live inventory of the AI systems you actually run, derived from traces rather than maintained by hand.

Every model, provider and environment observed in your traces is inventoried automatically — so the list reflects production rather than what a spreadsheet last recorded. Ownership and risk tier are yours to set, and are preserved when the inventory refreshes.

### How to use it

1. Assign an owner to every system

Unowned systems are the usual audit finding. Owner completeness also feeds the Accountability dimension of the Trust Profile.

2. Set risk tier where it differs from the default

Risk tier is how you signal that a system is higher-stakes than its traffic volume suggests.

3. Refresh after a launch

The inventory rebuilds on a schedule; Refresh pulls it forward when you have just shipped something and want it reflected now.

sections.title: Data Governance
sections.text:
## Data Governance

Where your data actually flows — provider × region × environment — alongside the residency and no-train policy.

Flows are derived from traces, so this reflects observed behaviour rather than intended architecture. The policy editor records the regions you consider approved and your no-train position, and every change is captured in the Audit Trail.

Recorded and audited, not enforced: AgentGuard records and audits the residency policy. It does not currently enforce it in the request path, so adherence here is observed, not guaranteed. Use the flow table to detect out-of-region traffic; do not rely on this page to prevent it.

### How to use it

1. Record the policy you actually operate under

Set the approved regions and no-train position. Globs are supported, so in-* covers a whole region family.

2. Compare the policy against observed flows

The flow table is the check. Any provider or region outside your approved list is a finding to chase in Trace Explorer.

sections.title: Audit Trail
sections.text:
## Audit Trail

Every governance-relevant event, in an append-only record you can prove has not been altered.

Configuration changes, access events, guardrail decisions and evaluation results are normalised into one stream. Entries are hash-chained: each links to the one before it, so removing or editing an entry breaks the chain in a way the integrity check detects.

### How to use it

1. Verify integrity before exporting anything

The integrity indicator re-computes the chain and compares it against stored checkpoints. Verify first, then export — an auditor will ask.

2. Filter to the window under review

Audit reviews are almost always period-scoped. Narrow the window before reading, rather than scrolling.

What is chained: The chain covers what was observed — the event, its time, its subject and its outcome. It deliberately excludes which compliance controls an event maps to, because that mapping is revised as frameworks are added. Re-classifying a control is not tampering and must not look like it.

sections.title: Common questions
sections.text:
## Common questions

Q: Why does every framework say “Not Assessed”?
A: No runtime evidence has reached the selected window. Coverage is derived from guardrail decisions, evaluation results and observed model inventory — none of which exist until traffic flows through the SDK. Widening the date range is worth trying; if it stays empty, start with Onboarding.

Q: I enabled a guardrail but its control is still a gap. What is wrong?
A: Nothing, most likely — the guardrail has not run yet. Coverage counts observed decisions, not configuration, so a guardrail that is switched on but has seen no traffic produces no evidence. Send a request through it and re-check. This is also why the OWASP page can show green while Compliance shows a gap.

Q: A control says “Out of scope”. Can I do something about it?
A: No, and that is deliberate. Out-of-scope means the control cannot be proven from runtime behaviour at all — training-data provenance, for example, or a capability that is not built yet. Rather than leave it as a permanent gap you have no way to close, it is excluded from the coverage denominator entirely.

Q: What makes a control “Partial” rather than covered?
A: The right kind of evidence is flowing, but not the specific signal that control needs — guardrails are recording decisions, but not the one this control is scoped to. Partial counts as half toward coverage.

Q: The audit-trail integrity check reports a problem. What now?
A: First establish whether the evidence period was re-baselined — a deliberate reset after a change to how the chain is computed will show the same way as a genuine break. If no re-baseline happened, treat it as a security event and escalate: the record is meant to be append-only.

sections.title: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
sections.text:
Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)

How AgentGuard roles, scopes, and enforcement layers work — for operators, security teams, and developers extending the platform.

sections.title: What is RBAC in AgentGuard?
sections.text:
## What is RBAC in AgentGuard?

Role-based access control (RBAC) decides who can see and change data in your organization and projects. AgentGuard uses roles (bundles of permissions) and fine-grained scopes (individual capabilities like guardrails:read or compliance:export) so you can separate operators, auditors, and administrators without sharing one login.

Least privilege: Give people only the access they need — read-only viewers, day-to-day members, or full admins.

Defense in depth: Menus, pages, buttons, and API routes are all checked — hiding UI is not enough on its own.

AgentGuard modules: Security and Governance scopes are separate from core tracing and evaluation scopes.

Org + project: Organization roles set the baseline; project roles can narrow or extend access per project.

Who this is for: Operators assign roles when inviting teammates. Developers add scopes when shipping new features. Security teams design roles like Auditor that limit exposure to governance and quality data only.

sections.title: How access is decided
sections.text:
## How access is decided

Every request passes through a short stack of checks before data is returned or a mutation runs.

### Decision stack

- Authentication — valid session or API key for the project.

- Instance controls — some modules (e.g. Governance) can be disabled for the whole deployment.

- Plan entitlements — cloud plans may gate product modules such as evaluation or datasets.

- RBAC scopes — the user's role must include the scope required for the route, page, or API procedure.

### Organization vs project roles

Users belong to an organization with an org role (Owner, Admin, Member, Viewer). They can also have a project-specific role that overrides the org default for that project only. Setting a project role to None means the org role applies.

Org roles control billing, org settings, and inviting members. Project roles control tracing, guardrails, governance exports, and similar day-to-day work inside a project.

### Scopes, not booleans

Permissions are named resource:action strings — for example auditTrail:read or policyAsCode:CUD. Read scopes unlock navigation and GET-style APIs. CUD scopes unlock create, update, and delete. Export scopes unlock CSV/JSON downloads without granting edit rights.

Super admin: Users with the instance admin flag bypass project RBAC for support and operations. Do not rely on RBAC alone if every human on the instance has super-admin access.

sections.title: Built-in project roles
sections.text:
## Built-in project roles

AgentGuard ships with five fixed project roles, each a curated set of scopes. Organizations can also define their own custom roles with a hand-picked scope bundle — see the Auditor example below.

Role: Owner | Typical use: Account owner | Summary: Full access including project delete and member management.

Role: Admin | Typical use: Team lead / platform admin | Summary: Same project powers as Owner except org-level ownership transfer.

Role: Member | Typical use: Engineer / operator | Summary: Day-to-day CUD on traces, evals, datasets, red-team runs; read Security & Governance; export compliance and audit data; no guardrail config or governance admin mutations.

Role: Viewer | Typical use: Stakeholder / read-only | Summary: Read across tracing, evaluation, Security, and Governance; no CUD or exports (except what read scopes imply).

Role: None (inherit org) | Typical use: Per-project override off | Summary: Uses the organization role for this project.

### Custom roles

Beyond the five built-in roles, an org admin can define custom roles under Organization Settings → Custom Roles (requires the rbac-custom-roles entitlement). A custom role bundles any set of project scopes — grouped in the UI by feature area (Governance, Security, Evals / LLM-as-judge, Prompts, Datasets, …) — under a name you choose. It's assignable from the same Project Role dropdown as the built-in roles, and is an explicit override: it replaces the built-in role entirely rather than adding to it. See Example: build an Auditor role below for a worked walkthrough.

### Security scopes

Gate the Security sidebar: overview, guardrails, OWASP, incidents, red teaming, and targets.

Scope: securityOverview:read | Allows: Security overview dashboard

Scope: guardrails:read / guardrails:CUD | Allows: View vs configure guardrails

Scope: owasp:read | Allows: OWASP LLM Top 10 views

Scope: securityIncidents:read | Allows: Security incidents list

Scope: redTeam:read / redTeam:CUD / redTeam:export | Allows: View, run, and export red-team campaigns

Scope: redTeamTargets:read / redTeamTargets:CUD | Allows: View vs manage red-team targets

### Governance scopes

Gate the Governance sidebar: trust profile, compliance, policy-as-code, AI BOM, audit trail, and data governance.

Scope: governance:read / governance:CUD | Allows: Trust profile and rollup admin

Scope: compliance:read / compliance:export | Allows: Framework views and exports

Scope: policyAsCode:read / policyAsCode:CUD | Allows: Policy definitions and edits

Scope: aibom:read / aibom:CUD / aibom:export | Allows: AI BOM inventory

Scope: auditTrail:read / auditTrail:export | Allows: Immutable audit log

Scope: dataGovernance:read / dataGovernance:CUD | Allows: Data classification and retention rules

### Tracing & evaluation (quality)

Core observability and quality workflows use scopes such as project:read, TableViewPresets:read, datasets:read, evalJob:read, scores:CUD, and annotationQueues:read. Trace Explorer relies on project:read plus TableViewPresets:read, comments:read, and annotationQueues:read (all mandatory on custom roles) and product entitlements — there is no separate traces:read scope yet. Playground requires llmApiKeys:read (and optionally prompts:read to load prompts).

sections.title: Where permissions are enforced
sections.text:
## Where permissions are enforced

A feature is secure only when every layer agrees. AgentGuard applies RBAC at four places.

### Sidebar navigation

Each route in the app shell declares the scopes required to see it. If the user lacks any required scope (OR logic), the menu item is removed. Empty sidebar groups disappear automatically when all child routes are hidden.

### Page entry

Sensitive pages use the same scopes as the menu and show an access-denied state on direct URL access instead of leaking data.

### Buttons and exports

Create, toggle, save, and export controls check CUD or export scopes before rendering. Users without permission see a read-only experience.

### API and tRPC

Server handlers enforce the matching scope on every mutation and export. UI hiding is a convenience — API enforcement is the authority. Public REST routes use the same scope names via project API keys tied to a role.

### Project settings

Each tab under Project Settings maps to a dedicated scope. See Project settings tabs (#project-settings) for the full matrix (VIEWER vs MEMBER per tab).

Tip: When you add a new module, wire all four layers. Skipping API checks leaves a hole even if the menu entry is hidden.

sections.title: Project settings tabs
sections.text:
## Project settings tabs

Each tab under Project Settings requires a project scope. Tabs are hidden from the sidebar when the user lacks the scope, and direct URLs show an access-denied page.

Tab: General | URL slug: index | Required scope: project:read | VIEWER: Yes | MEMBER: Yes

Tab: API Keys | URL slug: api-keys | Required scope: apiKeys:read | VIEWER: No | MEMBER: View (CUD for create/delete)

Tab: LLM Connections | URL slug: llm-connections | Required scope: llmApiKeys:read | VIEWER: Yes | MEMBER: Yes

Tab: Model Definitions | URL slug: models | Required scope: models:CUD | VIEWER: No | MEMBER: No (Admin/Owner)

Tab: Protected Prompt Labels | URL slug: protected-prompt-labels | Required scope: promptProtectedLabels:CUD | VIEWER: No | MEMBER: No

Tab: Scores Configs | URL slug: scores | Required scope: scoreConfigs:CUD | VIEWER: No | MEMBER: Yes

Tab: Members | URL slug: members | Required scope: projectMembers:read | VIEWER: No | MEMBER: Yes

Tab: Integrations | URL slug: integrations | Required scope: integrations:CRUD | VIEWER: No | MEMBER: No (Admin/Owner)

Tab: Exports | URL slug: exports | Required scope: batchExports:read | VIEWER: No | MEMBER: Yes

Tab: Batch Actions | URL slug: batch-actions | Required scope: datasets:CUD | VIEWER: No | MEMBER: Yes

Tab: Notifications | URL slug: notifications | Required scope: project:read | VIEWER: Yes | MEMBER: Yes

### How it is enforced

- A central settings tab scope map defines which scope each tab requires.

- Each tab and direct URL to a tab is gated — users without the scope see access denied instead of partial content.

- Dangerous actions inside General (rename, delete, transfer) still require project:update or project:deleteseparately from merely opening the tab.

Org settings: Organization member management lives under Organization Settings and uses organizationMembers:read — separate from project Members tab scopes.

Production tip: Assign project VIEWER for auditors and stakeholders who should not change API keys, score configs, exports, or member roles. They still see General, LLM Connections (read), and personal notification preferences.

sections.title: Assigning roles in the UI
sections.text:
## Assigning roles in the UI

Project admins and org admins manage membership from Settings → Members.

- Open Organization settings → Members or Project settings → Members.

- Invite by email or change an existing member's organization role.

- Optionally set a project role that overrides the org role for one project (useful for contractors or auditors).

- You can only assign roles at or below your own level — an Admin cannot promote someone to Owner.

### API keys

Project API keys inherit the scopes of the role selected when the key was created. Use read-only keys for integrations that only ingest traces; use Member keys for automation that creates scores or runs evals.

Audit: Role changes are recorded in organization audit logs when audit logging is enabled. Pair RBAC with Governance audit trail for project-level security events.

sections.title: Developer guide — adding a new module
sections.text:
## Developer guide — adding a new module

Follow this checklist when you ship a feature that needs its own permission.

- Register new scopes in the project scope list (e.g. myFeature:read, myFeature:CUD).

- Add the new scopes to a group in the scope-group registry (or a new group) — a coverage test fails the build if a scope is left ungrouped, since the custom-role scope picker relies on every scope having a group.

- Map those scopes to each built-in role in the role access matrix — decide what Viewer, Member, Admin, and Owner receive.

- Attach required scopes to navigation route definitions so the sidebar hides items the user cannot open.

- For project settings tabs, add the tab to the settings scope map and wrap tab content in the settings tab access gate.

- Wrap feature pages in the page access gate using the read scope for that module.

- Guard mutations in API handlers with the matching CUD or export scope — the server must reject unauthorized calls even if the UI is hidden.

- Hide create, export, and other destructive controls in the UI when the user lacks the corresponding scope.

### Where to wire permissions

- Project scope definitions and the role-to-scope matrix

- Application navigation and route metadata

- Shared client and server access-check helpers

- Project settings tab scope registry

Organization scopes: Billing and org-wide settings use a separate organization scope model and organization-level route guards — independent from project scopes.

sections.title: Example: build an Auditor role (Governance + Evals only)
sections.text:
## Example: build an Auditor role (Governance + Evals only)

Many teams want auditors who can review governance evidence and eval/quality signals without touching security configuration or production data.

Custom roles let an org admin bundle any set of project scopes into a role they name themselves — no code change or migration required. Here's how to build an "Auditor" role scoped to just Governance and Evals / LLM-as-judge.

### Walkthrough

- Go to Organization Settings → Custom Roles (visible if your plan includes the rbac-custom-roles entitlement) and select Create role.

- Name it Auditor and add an optional description, e.g. "Read + export access to Governance and Evals, nothing else."

- In the scope picker, use the group-level checkbox to select everything under Governance and Evals / LLM-as-judge. Leave every other group (Security, Prompts, Members, API Keys, Project Settings, …) unchecked.

- Save. The role now appears alongside Owner/Admin/Member/Viewer in the Project Role dropdown on the Members table.

- Open Members for the target project and set the person's Project Role to Auditor. This is an explicit override — it replaces whatever their org role would have granted on that project, it does not add on top of it.

### Scopes this role grants

Area: Governance | Modules: Compliance, AI BOM, audit trail, policy-as-code, data governance | Scopes selected: All Governance group scopes (read + export + CUD, or read-only if you prefer a stricter reviewer)

Area: Evaluation (quality) | Modules: Eval templates, eval jobs/runs, default eval model | Scopes selected: All Evals / LLM-as-judge group scopes

### What this role does not grant

- Entire Security group (guardrails, red-teaming, OWASP, incidents)

- Project settings, API key management, member CUD

- Prompt CUD, dataset CUD, model/tool CUD

- Anything in project:read's neighboring groups you didn't explicitly check — the picker is opt-in per scope, so an unchecked group grants nothing

Who can create custom roles: Creating, editing, and assigning custom roles requires the organizationMembers:CUD scope — today held only by OWNER/ADMIN org roles — plus the rbac-custom-roles entitlement. An assigner also cannot grant a custom role that includes scopes they don't themselves hold on that project.

sections.title: FAQ & troubleshooting
sections.text:
## FAQ & troubleshooting

Menu item missing: Confirm the user's project role includes the scopes declared on the route, the product module is entitled on your plan, and instance controls allow the module.

Page loads but button missing: CUD/export scopes are separate from read scopes. Member may see guardrails but cannot toggle them without guardrails:CUD.

API 403 with valid key: API keys are scoped to the role at creation time. Re-create the key or upgrade the member role if scopes changed.

Viewer sees Security: Viewer currently includes Security and Governance read scopes. For a governance-only persona, create a custom role (Organization Settings → Custom Roles) scoped to just the groups you want — e.g. Governance + Evals / LLM-as-judge, per the Auditor example above — and assign it instead of Viewer. Editing Viewer's own scope map is still an option but affects every Viewer in the organization.

Custom Roles tab missing: The Custom Roles settings tab and the custom-role options in the role dropdowns are hidden unless the organization's plan includes the rbac-custom-roles entitlement.

More guides: Onboarding (/docs/onboarding)

sections.title: Authentication
sections.text:
Authentication

Sign-in providers, session timeouts, logout revocation, and how API keys differ from browser sessions.

sections.title: Authentication overview
sections.text:
## Authentication overview

AgentGuard separates human console access (browser sessions via NextAuth) from machine access (project API keys and SDK credentials). Both are scoped to organizations and projects, but they use different token lifecycles and revocation models.

Console vs API: The web UI uses short-lived JWT session cookies. SDKs and automation use public API keys with scopes inherited from the role chosen at key creation. See RBAC (/docs/rbac) for permission details.

sections.title: Sign-in methods
sections.text:
## Sign-in methods

Identity providers are enabled through environment variables. Only configured providers appear on the sign-in page.

Method: Email + password | Configuration: Default credentials provider | Notes: Disable with AUTH_DISABLE_USERNAME_PASSWORD=true

Method: Magic link / email | Configuration: Email provider + SMTP | Notes: Passwordless invite and sign-in flows

Method: Google, GitHub, GitLab | Configuration: AUTH_*_CLIENT_ID / secret pairs | Notes: Social and enterprise Git hosting

Method: Azure AD, Okta, Auth0, Keycloak | Configuration: OIDC provider env blocks | Notes: Enterprise SSO

Method: Custom OIDC | Configuration: AUTH_CUSTOM_* | Notes: Any compliant identity provider

### Signup and invites

New users typically join through an organization invite. Instance-wide self-signup can be restricted with AUTH_DISABLE_SIGNUP=true. Account linking between providers is controlled per provider (e.g. AUTH_GOOGLE_ALLOW_ACCOUNT_LINKING).

Operator tip: Configure only the providers your organization uses. Unused provider buttons confuse users and widen the attack surface if credentials are left in env files.

sections.title: Session lifecycle
sections.text:
## Session lifecycle

Console sessions use JWT strategy with HttpOnly cookies — not server-side session stores for every request.

### Default timeouts

Variable: AUTH_SESSION_MAX_AGE | Default: 60 minutes | Meaning: Sliding idle window — session expires after inactivity

Variable: AUTH_SESSION_UPDATE_AGE | Default: 5 minutes | Meaning: How often an active session JWT is renewed

Variable: AUTH_SESSION_ABSOLUTE_MAX_AGE | Default: 480 minutes (8 h) | Meaning: Hard cap from login; forces re-auth even if active

### How refresh works

- User signs in → JWT issued with sid (a custom session id, stable for the life of the login), session timestamps.

- While the tab is open, the client refetches /api/auth/session every five minutes (and on focus).

- When updateAge elapses, NextAuth re-issues the JWT with a new expiry.

- On renewal, sid is kept unchanged — rotating it on every renewal and denylisting the previous value races with in-flight requests from a tab that just woke up idle, causing spurious logouts. Logout is what denylists the current sid, once.

- Idle longer than MAX_AGE or absolute max → user must sign in again.

sections.title: Logout and token revocation
sections.text:
## Logout and token revocation

Logout must invalidate the session server-side — not only delete the browser cookie.

### JWT denylist

Each session JWT carries a unique sid, stable for the life of that login (not the standard jti claim, which NextAuth's own JWT encoder regenerates on every cookie re-encode — a same-named custom field would be silently overwritten on each renewal). On logout, AgentGuard records that sid (and a SHA-256 fingerprint of the raw cookie for legacy tokens) in Redis until the token would have expired. Subsequent requests with that cookie are rejected at:

- /api/auth/session — returns empty session

- tRPC and SSR auth — treated as unauthenticated

- Page proxy — redirect to sign-in

Multi-device: Revocation is per session. Logging out on one laptop does not invalidate sessions on other devices — each device has its own sid.

### Redis dependency

Denylist writes and checks use Redis. If Redis is unavailable, the system fails open with a warning log so login and logout still work — but stolen-cookie protection is weakened. Keep Redis healthy in production.

sections.title: API keys vs browser sessions
sections.text:
## API keys vs browser sessions

Choose the right credential for each integration.

Credential: Session cookie | Used for: Web console, tRPC from browser | Lifetime: Short-lived JWT with refresh | Revocation: Logout denylist + expiry

Credential: Project API key | Used for: SDK ingestion, public REST API | Lifetime: Until deleted or rotated | Revocation: Delete or invalidate key in settings

Credential: Organization keys | Used for: Org-level automation (where enabled) | Lifetime: Until deleted | Revocation: Admin rotation in org settings

RBAC: API keys inherit scopes from the project role selected at creation. A read-only automation should use a Viewer-scoped key, not an Admin key.

sections.title: Security checklist for operators
sections.text:
## Security checklist for operators

Review these settings when hardening a production deployment.

- Confirm AUTH_SESSION_* values match organizational policy (idle 60 min, absolute 8 h by default).

- Enable only required SSO providers; disable username/password if SSO is mandatory.

- Verify logout revokes sessions (replay stolen cookie after sign-out should fail).

- Run Redis for JWT denylist in production; monitor Redis availability.

- Rotate API keys on role changes; avoid long-lived Admin keys in CI.

- Pair session controls with RBAC (/docs/rbac) so least-privilege applies inside the console too.

sections.title: FAQ
sections.text:
## FAQ

Session expired quickly: Check AUTH_SESSION_MAX_AGE (idle) and AUTH_SESSION_ABSOLUTE_MAX_AGE (hard cap). Active users should see refresh every five minutes via updateAge.

Still logged in after logout elsewhere: Each browser session is independent. Org-wide forced logout of all devices requires additional operational tooling beyond per-session denylist.

API 401 with valid key: Keys do not auto-upgrade when roles change — create a new key or confirm the member's project role includes required scopes.
